weaknesses: The central claim that discrete tokenization is responsible for the gains is not established. There is no continuous, non-quantized version of the same architecture and training pipeline; comparisons against BIOT and LaBraM confound tokenization with architecture, capacity, and objectives. Because the encoder immediately maps indices back to continuous embeddings without reducing sequence length, the claimed parameter and complexity benefits also cannot be attributed to discretization without FLOP, memory, latency, or storage measurements.

The claimed scalability and generalization are largely untested. A separate tokenizer and encoder are pretrained and fine-tuned within each dataset; there is no cross-dataset transfer, shared vocabulary, zero/few-shot adaptation, unseen montage or sampling-rate evaluation, or controlled test of missing and variable channels. This falls short of the motivating claim of a broadly reusable EEG tokenizer.

The frequency-learning analysis appears technically invalid as described: it applies a DFT and spectral entropy to sequences of categorical token IDs. Token IDs are nominal and can be arbitrarily permuted without changing the model, while such a permutation can drastically change the reported spectrum. Thus Figure 4 does not demonstrate that the tokens preserve richer EEG frequency information.

Tokenizer pretraining permits a major shortcut: the complete raw waveform is supplied while masked STFT values are reconstructed, even though those spectral values are deterministically obtainable from the raw window. Consequently, the objective does not force inference from unmasked spectral context, and the presented ablations do not establish that the proposed frequency pathway learns the asserted motifs.

The token-quality evidence is weak. Low utilization may indicate codebook collapse rather than compactness; the proposed class-token uniqueness statistic is sensitive to class/sample frequency and rare tokens; and neither statistic has uncertainty estimates. Retrieval omits important continuous-representation baselines and protocol details, while interpretability rests on a few selected examples from only two classes without expert assessment or quantitative controls.

Several headline gains are small relative to their reported standard deviations, especially on TUEV, yet no paired tests or confidence intervals support repeated claims of significance. The CHB-MIT test set contains only subjects 22–23, so five optimization seeds do not capture patient-level variability and provide limited evidence of clinical generalization.

Reproducibility remains insufficient despite the hyperparameter tables: no code or trained artifacts are provided, and key details are missing, including loss weights, exact masking probabilities, EMA settings, the specific linear-attention implementation, hyperparameter search spaces and budgets, selection criteria, class sampling, and whether every unsupervised stage was restricted to training splits. The STFT specification is also internally unclear: a one-sided 200-point FFT normally yields 101 bins, whereas the decoder output is listed as 100.

The clinical framing lacks discussion of demographic bias, dataset shift, privacy, external validation, and safeguards against interpreting the selected token motifs as clinically validated biomarkers. Overall, the method is promising, but the unsupported causal claims and invalid token-frequency analysis are substantial enough that the paper is not yet competitive for acceptance.

Repeating optimization seeds on a fixed split does not establish population-level generalization. Reported p-values lack the statistical test, unit of replication, confidence intervals, and multiple-comparison treatment.

Several claims conflict with the tables. In multi-dataset CHB-MIT evaluation, BIOT has substantially higher balanced accuracy than the proposed model. The supplied manuscript contains an empty code URL despite claiming that source code and pretrained weights are available. Hyperparameter-search spaces, trial counts, selection criteria, and explicit assurances that test subjects were excluded from all unsupervised pretraining and tuning are also absent.

The overall contribution is an incremental combination of standard STFT, transformer, masking, and VQ components. weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central claim that discretization is beneficial. There is no matched continuous-embedding version of the same encoder and downstream Transformer, nor matched alternatives such as k-means/VQ on STFT features. Consequently, gains may arise from the dual-path encoder, reconstruction pretraining, downstream architecture, or tuning rather than from tokenization itself. Comparisons against structurally different systems such as LaBraM do not resolve this confound.

The tokenizer objective may leak its reconstruction target. Masking is formally applied only to the spectrogram S, while the corresponding raw patches x are apparently supplied unmasked to the temporal path; because S is deterministically computed from x, the model can recover masked spectral content directly. Moreover, the claimed temporal Transformer has no positional encoding, making it permutation-equivariant and unable to model temporal order as claimed.

Evidence for the proposed joint temporal-frequency mechanism is weak. Part of the token analysis is technically invalid or insufficiently defined. Applying a DFT and spectral entropy to sequences of categorical token IDs is not invariant to arbitrary codebook-index permutations and therefore cannot establish frequency learning. The class-uniqueness score is highly sensitive to vocabulary occupancy and sample count and lacks a permutation/null baseline. Approximately 90% of the 8192-entry vocabulary is unused, which may indicate codebook collapse rather than desirable compactness. The qualitative motif examples are selected post hoc and lack expert validation.

Several claims overstate the tables. TFM does not outperform every baseline on every metric—for example, its multi-dataset CHB-MIT balanced accuracy is 0.6471 versus BIOT's 0.7068. Table 9's statement that 93% of metric cells improve appears inconsistent with the displayed values: 31 of 36 cells improve, approximately 86%. Large relative percentages such as the 147% gain also amplify very weak baseline values.

The cross-device evidence is too narrow for the claimed scalability: EESM23 contains only 10 subjects, with two test subjects under one fixed split, and the models are fine-tuned rather than evaluated zero-shot. Five optimization seeds do not measure uncertainty over subject selection. There are no ear-EEG-specific baselines, leave-one-subject-out evaluation, or tests on additional devices. The full downstream model also uses channel embeddings, so the complete pipeline is not inherently channel-agnostic.

Baseline and statistical protocols are insufficiently controlled. Results mix published numbers with reproductions under different pretraining corpora, while the proposed model receives extensive Ray Tune optimization whose search spaces, trial counts, and compute are unreported. The tests producing p=1.5e-4 and p=0.02 are unspecified, treat only five seeds as replicates, and provide no multiple-comparison correction or subject-level confidence intervals.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Missing details include mask ratios, alpha/beta loss weights, EMA decay, straight-through quantization, decoder specification, dataset sampling during multi-corpus training, and many fine-tuning settings. There is also a dimensional inconsistency: n_fft=200 with one-sided STFT yields 101 bins, whereas the decoder outputs 100, with no stated bin removal. Although code and weights are claimed, the supplied PDF contains no repository URL or hyperlink.

The novelty positioning omits sufficiently direct comparisons with prior discrete EEG encoders such as DeWave-like approaches and generic neural signal codecs. The paper also lacks an ethics or broader-impact discussion despite using sensitive clinical EEG and motivating eventual cross-device clinical deployment; privacy, demographic bias, failure costs, and intended-use limitations should be addressed.
